stories.headline: G N Lone Hanjura accuses NC Govt of failing to deliver on election promises
stories.title: G N Lone Hanjura accuses NC Govt of failing to deliver on election promises
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 20: Jammu and Kashmir Peoples Democratic Party (JKPDP) General Secretary (Organisation), Adv. Ghulam Nabi Lone Hanjura, Tuesday criticised the present National Conference-led government, alleging that it has failed to deliver on its promises even after completing two years in office. Hanjura, in a statement, said that the government has failed to fulfil the promises made to the people in its election manifesto, leaving them disappointed with its performance. He said that people are facing numerous difficulties and growing concerns over the government's handling of public issues, while promises made during the elections remain unfulfilled. He emphasised that the people of Jammu and Kashmir deserve accountable governance, a responsive administration, and concrete action on issues affecting their daily lives. He stressed that electoral promises must translate into tangible results on the ground rather than remain confined to political commitments. Hanjura presided over a meeting of district and zonal presidents of Kashmir Province to discuss various organisational matters, review the party's grassroots functioning, and strengthen coordination among party units across the region. The meeting was Attended By Mohammad Khursheed Alam General Secretary JKPDP, Mohammad Iqbal Trumboo Spokesperson JKPDP, Arif Laigroo, District Presidents Mohammad Afzal Wani, G.M. Shahoori, Ab. Qayoom Bhat, Zaffar Ullah Wani, Adv. Sheikh Javaid, Zahoor Ahmed Rather, Mohammad Yaseen Bhat and Aijaz Ahmed Mir; along with all Zonal Presidents. The meeting deliberated on key organisational issues, with particular emphasis on strengthening the party's presence at the grassroots level, enhancing public outreach, and ensuring that party representatives remain closely connected with the people and their concerns. Addressing the meeting, Hanjura stressed the importance of maintaining regular public contact and remaining accessible to people in their respective areas. He said that party representatives must understand the day-to-day difficulties faced by the public, listen to their grievances, and make sincere efforts to help address their concerns through appropriate channels. He underlined that a political organisation must remain firmly rooted among the people and consistently raise issues affecting different sections of society. He emphasised that direct interaction with the public is essential to understanding local problems, identifying pressing concerns, and ensuring that people's voices are heard. Hanjura also stressed the need for stronger coordination between district and zonal leadership, stating that effective organisational functioning requires regular communication, active grassroots engagement, and a sustained commitment to public service. The meeting also discussed ways to strengthen the party's organisational network across Kashmir Province and ensure that its activities remain connected with the aspirations and concerns of the people. The meeting concluded with an emphasis on strengthening the party's organisational structure, maintaining a continuous presence on the ground, and intensifying engagement with the public to understand and address their genuine grievances.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Quietly Rewrote Law On Alibi
stories.title: Supreme Court Quietly Rewrote Law On Alibi
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: A quiet but consequential shift just occurred in Indian criminal procedure, and it happened in a case that, on its surface, looks like a routine mercy for a soldier.

State of Uttar Pradesh (Criminal Appeal arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 2939 of 2026, decided on 11 August 2026), Rahul, a Border Security Force jawan, was posted on the Indo-Bangladesh border when his wife died at her matrimonial home in Meerut.
He, his parents, and other relatives were booked for dowry death.
His parents went to trial and, after years of proceedings, were acquitted, the prosecution couldn't prove its case.
The Allahabad High Court held that an alibi is a matter for trial, not something a court can weigh on paper, before evidence is tested, before witnesses are cross-examined.

The Supreme Court disagreed, reviving a line with far-reaching implications: that where a defence document is of "sterling and unimpeachable quality" and it "completely demolishes the prosecution case," the High Courts can quash such proceedings before trial even begins.
This instance unsettles a rule that has protected criminal trials for decades, and every criminal lawyer now has reason to pay attention.

An alibi doesn't just deny guilt; it claims physical impossibility, "I could not have done this, because I was elsewhere." Because that claim can be faked as easily as it can be true, the law has always required it to be proved "with absolute certainty," at trial, where the document can be tested, and the other side gets a real chance to challenge it.
A court asked to quash a case beforehand has traditionally been told not to play judge on a paper nobody has had the chance to contest.
This idea that some documents are too solid to argue about did not begin with this particular case.
It traces back to 1992, when the Supreme Court in State of Haryana.
